title: One Body, Many Gifts, a New Self
summary: Paul urges his readers to walk worthy of their calling by keeping the unity of the Spirit: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all. The ascended Christ has given the church apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers to equip the saints so the whole body grows to maturity. Believers must no longer live as the Gentiles do but put off the old self and put on the new, which shows in truthful speech, controlled anger, honest work, words that build up, and forgiveness modeled on God's.
story: The letter turns here. Chapters 1 to 3 told what God has done: chosen, redeemed, raised, and united a people in Christ. Chapters 4 to 6 tell how that people should live. The word then in verse 1 marks the hinge; the commands grow out of the gifts. Paul begins with unity, the natural result of chapter 2's one new humanity, then describes how Christ equips the church to grow, and then describes the moral change that belongs to those who have learned Christ. The chapter sets out the pattern that continues into chapter 5: put off what belongs to the old life, put on what belongs to the new.
historical:
Paul again writes as a prisoner (v. 1). The Gentile readers came from cities where religion and morality were loosely connected. Worship of the gods involved sacrifices and festivals but did not usually demand a changed moral life, and sexual license, drunkenness at feasts, and cheating in business were widely tolerated. Paul's description of the Gentile way of life in verses 17 to 19 reflects a Jewish view of the pagan world, but also something many ancient moralists themselves lamented.

The list of leaders in verse 11 tells us something about the church's early organization. Apostles were those sent by the risen Christ, and prophets were believers who spoke messages from God to the congregation; together they are called the foundation of the church (2:20). Evangelists spread the gospel (Philip is called one in Acts 21:8). Pastors and teachers cared for and instructed local congregations. Scholars debate whether pastors and teachers are two roles or one, since the Greek grammar links them closely; many think they describe one office with two aspects.
cultural:
Clothing imagery runs through verses 22 to 24. To put off the old self and put on the new was a picture any reader understood: taking off one garment and putting on another. Some scholars connect the image with early baptismal practice, in which new believers may have removed their old clothes before baptism and put on new ones after, though the evidence for this practice is mostly later than Paul.

The instruction about stealing (v. 28) is striking in its positive turn. The thief should not simply stop; he should work with his own hands in order to share with those in need. Manual labor was often looked down on by the educated elite of the Greek and Roman world, but Paul himself worked as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3) and commends such work as a means of generosity. The saying about not letting the sun set on anger (v. 26) reflects a common ancient view that disputes should be settled before the day's end; compare Deuteronomy 24:15 on paying a worker before sunset.
literary: The chapter has two main movements. Verses 1 to 16 are about unity and growth. The sevenfold confession of verses 4 to 6 (one body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, God and Father) may draw on early Christian creedal language. Verse 8 quotes Psalm 68:18, a psalm of God's victorious ascent to his sanctuary; where the Hebrew speaks of receiving gifts, Paul says the ascended one gave gifts, a reading also found in an Aramaic paraphrase of the Psalms. Verses 9 and 10 comment on the quotation: the one who ascended first descended, which interpreters take as the incarnation, Christ's death and burial, or the Spirit's coming at Pentecost. Verses 17 to 32 contrast the old and new ways of life, with each command followed by a reason. The body image (vv. 12-16) combines growth, connection, and each part doing its work.

outline.t: Walk worthy: keep the unity of the Spirit
Gifts to equip the saints and build up the body
Put off the old self, put on the new
The new life in speech, anger, work, and forgiveness

doctrines.note: The church is one body with one Spirit, one Lord, and one Father. Its unity is given by God and must be kept by humility, gentleness, and patience. Christ gives leaders not to do all the ministry but to equip every believer for it, so the whole body grows.

The Spirit creates the church's unity (v. 3), and believers can grieve him by sinful speech and behavior (v. 30). The Spirit is personal: only a person can be grieved. He is also the seal who marks believers for the day of redemption.

The new self is created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness (v. 24). Holiness is not simply avoiding wrong but actively doing good: speaking truth, working to give, building others up, and forgiving.
The confession of verses 4 to 6 moves through one Spirit, one Lord, and one God and Father of all, reflecting the threefold shape of Christian faith that the church later confessed as the Trinity.

words.note: Henotes, unity or oneness. It appears in verse 3 (the unity of the Spirit) and verse 13 (unity in the faith). Paul does not tell believers to create unity but to keep what the Spirit has made, and to grow toward its fullness. Unity here is not uniformity; it holds together many different gifts.

Poimen, shepherd. This is the only place in the New Testament where the word is used for a church leader, and it is the source of the English word pastor. Elsewhere it describes Jesus as the good shepherd (John 10:11). Leaders are to care for God's flock under the chief Shepherd.

Apotithemi, to put off or lay aside, used for taking off clothing. Believers are to put off the old self and its deceitful desires (v. 22) and put off falsehood (v. 25). Change is described as a decisive act rather than gradual improvement alone.

Lupeo, to grieve or cause sorrow. Do not grieve the Holy Spirit (v. 30) echoes Isaiah 63:10, where Israel rebelled and grieved God's Holy Spirit. The Spirit is not an impersonal force but a person who can be saddened by his people's sin.

christ: Christ appears in this chapter as the ascended Lord who gives gifts to his people. He descended and ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things (v. 10), and from that position he equips the church. The goal of the church's growth is the full measure of the stature of Christ (v. 13), and the body grows up into him who is the head (v. 15). Believers learned Christ, were taught in him, and the truth is in Jesus (vv. 20-21). The final command ties everything back to the gospel: forgive one another as God in Christ forgave you (v. 32). Christian ethics in this chapter is the life of Christ worked out in his people.

hard.q: Are apostles and prophets, and gifts like prophecy, still given today?
hard.a:
Christians disagree about this, and the question touches several texts beyond this chapter. Many in the Reformed and some other traditions hold a cessationist view: apostles and prophets were foundational (2:20), given for the church's first generation to establish its teaching, and once the New Testament was complete these roles, along with miraculous gifts, ceased. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, and many others often called continuationists, hold that all the gifts continue until Christ returns, since the purpose Paul gives, building up the body until we all reach unity and maturity (v. 13), has not yet been fulfilled. Between these are positions that see prophecy continuing in a different form from Scripture, or that see apostleship continuing in a broader sense of missionary church-planting while the foundational apostles of Christ were unique.

Whatever their view, Christians agree on the chapter's main point: the risen Christ gives gifts to his church so that every member is equipped to serve, and the goal is a mature, united body speaking the truth in love.

questions: Paul says leaders are given to equip the saints for works of ministry. What ministry has God equipped you to do in the body?
Which of the commands in verses 25 to 32 comes hardest to you, and why do you think Paul gives a reason for each one?
Verse 32 grounds forgiveness in the way God has forgiven us in Christ. How does that change the way you think about someone who has wronged you?
